# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–39 (Updated 2026-10-13, Final Revision 10)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Spring of tenth year after Waterloo (1831). Story spans from Sunday, 26th April dinner (Chapters 1–35) through Chapter 36 (winter into summer) to Chapters 37–38 (spring/early summer) to **Chapter 39 (autumn of tenth year)**. Emperor of China dinner scheduled Monday, 8th July; election for Westminster borough Tuesday, 9th July. Chapters 37–38 set in Harrowgate hill farms, coastal towns, Dunholt village, Staveton harbor town, transitions to London and Liverpool. Chapter 39 set in village of Yarlton.
- **Key Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane, Beargarden Club, Bruton Street, Queen's Gate, Islington, City Road Music-Hall, Cannon Street Hotel, Euston Square, Liverpool); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Southend; Harrowgate; Lowestoft; Dunholt; Staveton; Gulton; Dunwick; Salford; Yarlton; coastal towns; rural areas (Sheep's Acre Farm, etc.).

## Major Deaths
John Sedley, Mr. Osborne, Joseph Sedley, Colonel Rawdon Crawley, Sir Pitt, Wevie Lindner (died winter, buried Salmere). Conar Hollett (drowned crossing estuary at Gulton; no body seen; Halan Hollett reported it at inn).

## Rebecca's Arc
Never became Lady Crawley; styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon) receives allowance but refuses to see her. Appears wealthy at Bath/Cheltenham, busies herself with piety and Charity Lists.

## Amelia and William Dobbin
Married at Ostend; Amelia initiated encounter. Dobbin quit service, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; daughter Jane his pride.

## Lady Carbury and Family

**Lady Carbury**: Welbeck Street resident. Authored "Criminal Queens." Crushed by "Evening Pulpit" review; praised by "Morning Breakfast Table" (Mr. Broune). Rejected Mr. Broune's proposal via letter; full of regrets; in debt. **Overdrawing her account at bank (Chapter 38). Chapter 39: A miserable woman—discovered Felix's failed elopement plan; helped him to bed early morning Wednesday after he arrived drunk at 6–7 A.M., fell in gutter, soiled and intoxicated.**

**Felix Carbury**: Director of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway. Won £2,000 from Lord Grasslough, £400 from Miles Grendall at gaming. **Chapter 38 (COMPLETED ELOPEMENT EXECUTION)**: Received £250 from Didon at Beargarden Club Monday 4 P.M. Upon receipt understood he must go to New York. Dined at club Monday evening, planned passage Tuesday under name "Walter Jones," spend Tuesday with Ruby at Music Hall, depart Wednesday 5 P.M. for Liverpool. Remained at Music Hall 10 P.M. to nearly midnight; Ruby did not appear; he was "very angry." Returned to club despite danger; found Dolly Longestaffe and Miles Grendall; whispered to Grendall to convert I.O.U.s to cash; Grendall refused. Had been drinking freely; held up scraps of paper, asked loudly if any would buy for five shillings in pound; called Grendall to card-room with Dolly as witness; Grendall again refused. **Wednesday morning, 5 A.M.: Felix departed Welbeck Street for Liverpool per schedule. PLAN FAILED: Elopement did not proceed. Chapter 38–39: Felix played at Beargarden till 4 A.M.; intoxicated and almost penniless; made unpleasant remarks about Miles Grendall (whom he accused of cheating at loo, appealing to Dolly as witness; claimed Grendall should be turned out of club); desperate row ensued; Dolly said he knew nothing about it; Lord Grasslough opined more than one person might be turned out. At 4 A.M. Felix left club with only change of ten-pound note; all luggage left in hall. Between 6–7 A.M. knocked at Welbeck Street door; latch-key inefficient; door locked (presumed he was at Liverpool); Lady Carbury opened door herself. He had fallen more than once, soiled with gutter, drunk. Mother exclaimed "Oh, Felix!" He lied, claiming "old shap stopped ush" (Melmotte); was drunk enough to lie; at that moment Melmotte fast asleep in Grosvenor Square, ignorant of plot. Felix stumbled upstairs; mother removed his clothes and boots; he fell asleep; she went to her room, miserable woman.**

**Henrietta Carbury**: Rejected Roger's suit (too young, age disparity). Paul returned "as still dear friend" within week, promising not to see her three months. Wore rose from Roger's room. Roger declared love anew (Chapter 32 evening); determination unshaken. Paul thoroughly in love with her. Chapter 36: Paul visited her at Welbeck Street; she told mother loves someone else and praises Roger as "rock of strength."

## Marie Melmotte and Elopement Attempt

**Marie Melmotte**: **Chapter 38 (COMPLETED ELOPEMENT EXECUTION)**: Sat up all night packing treasures with Didon; discussed American clergyman marrying them on board; planned wedding dress. Determined not to eat morning so no suspicion raised; would get refreshment at station. **6 A.M. Wednesday: Robert departed first with big boxes (ten pounds in pocket). Marie and Didon followed in second cab with smaller luggage. No impediment; civil man at Euston Square gave tickets in French. Got bad tea/uneatable food at station; Marie's restrained excitement so great food unnecessary. Took seats without impediment; departed.** As drew near Liverpool, Didon explained must not declare destination till ship at sea; need say nothing about steam packet till in cab. Big boxes directed "Madame Racine, Passenger to Liverpool"; Didon's similarly. Didon declared anxiety would not be over till ship moving. Marie sure dangers over if only Felix safe on board. **ELOPEMENT INTERCEPTED AT LIVERPOOL PLATFORM**: Upon train arrival, Marie hardly put foot on platform before gentleman (with another less-gentlemanly gentleman and nearby policeman) addressed her: "You, I think, are Miss Melmotte." Marie struck dumb, said nothing. Didon immediately became voluble in French, claiming young lady was Mademoiselle Racine, her niece, she was Madame Racine, knew nothing of Melmottes. Gentleman insisted, used her English, named her and Didon. Marie declared she spoke French; he countered "And English too." Gentleman told them to return to London; he would accompany them. Marie exclaimed "Ah, Didon, nous sommes perdues!" Didon asserted legality of their position; they had right to come to Liverpool, get in cab with luggage, had done nothing against laws. Gentleman spoke in low voice: cheque changed from father's house; father would pardon when she rejoined him; they could arrest her on cheque if forced; certainly would not let her board. If she traveled back to London with him, no unnecessary inconvenience. Gentleman telegraphed up to Grosvenor Square during journey. **At Euston Square met by one of Melmotte carriages. Marie taken home in carriage; box to follow in cab at interval so Grosvenor Square might not be aware (though it very soon knew all about it). Marie asked gentleman if he would come; he replied requested to see her home. Marie laughed: "All the people will wonder who you are." Gentleman thought Miss Melmotte would get through troubles without much suffering. Chapter 39: Marie aware she would be interrogated. Melmotte held her very hard, shook her while speaking, reminding her of his generosity (carriages, horses, bracelets, brooches, silks, gloves, everything else); declared "I've been very good to you." Marie shows determination: "I don't think that mamma cares. It's papa. I'd do it again to-morrow if I had the chance." Gentleman (not having expected such determination) looked at her. Marie continued: "I would. Why is a girl to be made to marry to please any one but herself? I won't. And it's very mean saying that I stole the money. I always take what I want, and papa never says anything about it."**

## Didon
Marie's attendant. **Chapter 38–39**: Executed elopement plan; presented Melmotte's cheque to bank, obtained £250, delivered to Felix at Beargarden Monday 4 P.M. Held tickets under name "Madame Racine." Departed 6 A.M. Wednesday with Marie in cab; faithful throughout; declared anxiety would not be over till ship moving. Intercepted at Liverpool; gave up game as regarded mistress; became voluble in French; asserted legality of position; plucked up courage for moment. To receive £50 before boarding (plan failed).

## Ruby Ruggles and Suitors

**Ruby Ruggles**: Pretty servant/maid to Mrs. Pipkin at Islington. Danced with Felix at City Road Music-Hall. When Felix refused marriage, Roger Carbury warned her forcefully; extracted promise not to see him again. Wrote Felix letter of regret; he replied tersely: Tuesday. Sought to attend Tuesday dance; Mrs. Pipkin refused, then reluctantly agreed. **Ruby attended Tuesday evening at Music Hall; Felix was there 10 P.M. to nearly midnight; did not connect (Felix noted her "non-appearance" and was "very angry").**

**John Crumb**: Country lover from Suffolk, "Bungay mealman." Chapter 35: Attempted to take Ruby's hand; Ruby fled. Rode to Carbury Hall. Chapter 37: Visited Roger, expressed anguish about Felix, willingness to "swing for it" if seduced. Roger assured him Ruby good, promised Mrs. Pipkin supervision. Resolved to send Mrs. Pipkin price of new blue cloak via Mixet's letter and money order.

**Daniel Ruggles**: Holds Sheep's Acre Farm. Violent; pulled Ruby by hair. Told Roger suitor should speak his mind.

**Mrs. Pipkin**: Ruby's aunt at Islington; lets lodgings. Feared Ruby would escape; reluctantly allowed Tuesday attendance at Music Hall.

## Paul Montague and Mrs. Winifrid Hurtle

**Paul's Crisis (Chapter 37)**: At Lowestoft, told Mrs. Hurtle he cannot join his lot with her—his heart elsewhere; friends warned him of her antecedents. Mrs. Hurtle responded with fury. Confessed she shot a man in Oregon; saved herself. Divorced Caradoc Hurtle (drunkard, scoundrel) under Kansas law on grounds of cruelty/drunkenness (he made no appearance; court granted). Questioned why condemned for protecting herself. Called him coward, said he trembles between her and Roger. Declared would not stay, return Monday, resolve what to do, seek means of punishing him.

**Mrs. Hurtle's Aftermath (Chapter 37–38)**: Fell on knees, flood of tears. Loved this young Englishman with heart of hearts. Ran over on vain chance after his letter. Knew Englishwomen would avoid her when past known; scorned/feared in eastern cities; name proverb for violence in far West. Hesitation in marriage arose from own conviction of unfitness; circumstances made her what she was; could not alter them. Gradually believed in his love, lost herself in it, told herself she would change. Almost known it could not be so. Returned from Lowestoft Monday; made trivial excuse to Mrs. Pipkin (windy, too cold, disliked hotel). Mrs. Pipkin glad to see her back. Has not sent letter in pocket-book; keeps it, at moments thinking to send it, at others telling herself never surrender last hope till every stone turned. Might still shame him into marriage. Promised Mrs. Pipkin she would speak to Ruby (though aware of unfitness—knew nothing of country, not single friend but Paul, ran after him with little discretion as Ruby after her lover). Paul returned to London by mail train evening, sure he would avoid meeting Mrs. Hurtle in railway-carriage.

## The Melmottes

**Augustus Melmotte**: Chairman, South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway. Chapter 37–38: Extremely busy with electioneering speeches, Committee members, dinner orders, commercial affairs. Told Felix entitled only to £600 shares now, will see it put right. Proposed Paul Mexican embassy; tone dubious to Paul. Expressed relief dinner would be over. Received Board meeting call; ran off to Cannon Street Hotel meeting. Chapter 38–39: Fast asleep in Grosvenor Square Wednesday morning, altogether ignorant of elopement plot when Felix stumbled home drunk; later interrogated Marie about cheque; held her very hard, shook her while reminding her of generosity.

## The Longestaffes

**Sir Merton Longestaffe**: Determined no London expenses. Desires to sell Pickering, disembarrass Caversham. Dolly refused consent unless half produce given to him.

**Adolphus (Dolly) Longestaffe**: Bruton Street rooms. Arrangement made: £5,000 pay off tradesmen's debts, leave him comfortably possessed; other £20,000 make property free. Returned demanding cheque on Melmotte's bank payable to his own. Has not received single ten-pound note. Threatens employment of Mr. Squercum if money not paid quickly. **Chapter 38–39: Present at club smoking-room Monday evening with Miles Grendall. When Felix accused Grendall of cheating at loo, appealed to Dolly as witness; Dolly said he knew nothing about it.**

**Georgiana Longestaffe**: Made protest against Melmottes. Following morning received invitation to stay with them. By Sunday present at Grosvenor Square.

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Scheme

**The Enterprise**: Railway from Salt Lake City through New Mexico/Arizona into Mexico, terminating Vera Cruz. Approximately 2,000 miles. Stock at par; shares sold at premium. Directors understood fortune made by floating shares, not building railway.

**London Directorate**: Melmotte (chairman), Lord Alfred Grendall, Sir Felix Carbury (now fled to America—or attempted to), Samuel Cohenlupe (MP for Staines), Lord Nidderdale, Paul Montague.

## Roger Carbury
Nearly forty. Never owed shilling he couldn't pay. Firmly opposed Melmotte connection on principle. Soft heart; knows Lady Carbury false and Felix worthless. Declared love to Henrietta anew; determination unshaken. Visited Ruby at Islington; warned her against Felix; extracted promise not to see him again; spoke to Mrs. Pipkin about late hours. Encountered Paul and Mrs. Hurtle at Lowestoft; greeted coldly; reproved Paul severely. Counselled marriage with her would be destruction. Upon Paul's return, expressed satisfaction: "Let her follow you, and bear it. Of course you must suffer the effects of your own imprudence."

## Minor Characters
**Lord Alfred Grendall**: Nearly overwhelmed by electioneering; nearly in rebellion. Burdened with seating arrangements.

**Miles Grendall**: Secretary to Melmotte. Does not pay debts of honour. **Chapter 38–39: Present at club smoking-room Monday evening with Dolly. Felix whispered petition to convert I.O.U.s to cash; Grendall refused, said no one playing that night, would be there tomorrow. Later when Felix accused him of cheating at loo (appealing to Dolly as witness) and claimed he should be turned out of club, desperate row ensued; Lord Grasslough opined perhaps more than one person ought to be turned out.**

**Robert** (servant): **Marie's man; departed 6 A.M. Wednesday with big boxes, ten pounds already in pocket; elopement intercepted.**

**Father John Barham**: Priest, Beccles.

**Sally Hockett**: Witnessed Daniel Ruggles pulling Ruby by hair.

**Mr. Squercum**: Lawyer threatened employment by Dolly.

**Provincial Figures (Chapters 37–39)**: Halan Hollett, Thivie Brackwood, Votho Brackwood, Brenelle Brackwood, Jozek Hollett, Garald Stenworth, Nylis Corrett, Rolde (child, Staveton), Orbin Stenworth, Ilrine Corrett, Feten Lindner, Manelle (quit Dunwick for Salford after quarrel), figures in Yarlton village.
